title: Rightsizing, Graviton & Serverless Cost Tuning
summary: Find over-provisioned compute, move to Graviton, and tune Lambda and containers for cost.
tldr: Order of operations: **turn off** what isn't used (schedules, hibernation), **rightsize** what's left (Compute Optimizer), **switch to Graviton**, and only then **commit** with Savings Plans or Reserved Instances.
**Compute Optimizer** uses utilization history to recommend sizes for EC2, Auto Scaling groups, EBS, Lambda, ECS on Fargate and RDS. It sees **memory** only if the **CloudWatch agent** publishes it.

**Graviton (Arm64)** gives better price performance on EC2, Fargate, Lambda, RDS/Aurora and ElastiCache. Interpreted languages usually move with little or no code change; native binaries need arm64 builds.
**Lambda** cost is memory × duration; use **Lambda Power Tuning** (or Compute Optimizer) to find the cheapest memory setting, and arm64 for a lower per-GB-second price.

keyFacts.text: EC2 doesn't report memory to CloudWatch by default. Install the CloudWatch agent so Compute Optimizer can rightsize memory-heavy fleets.
Price performance AWS quotes for Lambda functions on arm64 (Graviton2) versus x86. Test first; dependencies must ship arm64 builds.
Hibernation saves RAM to an **encrypted** EBS root volume, so long warm-ups survive a nightly stop and you pay only for storage overnight.
A T instance in unlimited mode with high CPU all day pays extra credit charges. A fixed-performance instance (for example m7g) is cheaper.
A dev box used 10 hours on weekdays runs about 30% of the week. Scheduling stop/start cuts its On-Demand compute bill by roughly 70%.

traps: Buying Savings Plans or RIs before rightsizing or moving to Graviton locks in the old, larger footprint.
Fargate Spot and EC2 Spot are wrong when the question says the service cannot tolerate interruption.
Switching a busy T instance to standard mode throttles it to baseline CPU, which degrades performance.
Changing an x86 instance to a Graviton type with the same AMI fails; Graviton needs an arm64 AMI.
Trusted Advisor's low-utilization check is CPU-based and coarse; Compute Optimizer gives specific, ML-based recommendations.
